text: Excerpt from the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat directive. Source: https://www.tbs-sct.canada.ca/pol/doc-eng.aspx?id=32592 Licence: Open Government Licence – Canada. Contains information licensed under the Open Government Licence – Canada. This file is an excerpt for retrieval, not the full instrument. Effective 1 April 2019. Page text consulted 2026-11-07.
section_path: Directive on Automated Decision-Making > Directive on Automated Decision-Making
licence: Open Government Licence – Canada

text: The objective of this directive is to ensure that automated decision systems are used in a manner that reduces risks to clients, departments and Canadian society, and leads to more efficient, accurate, consistent and interpretable decisions made pursuant to Canadian law. Decisions made by departments are to be data-driven and responsible, and comply with procedural fairness and due process requirements.
section_path: Directive on Automated Decision-Making > Directive on Automated Decision-Making > Section 4 Objectives
licence: Open Government Licence – Canada

text: Completing, approving and publishing the final results of an algorithmic impact assessment in an accessible format on the Open Government Portal prior to the production of any automated decision system. Reviewing, approving, and updating the published algorithmic impact assessment on a scheduled basis, including when the functionality or scope of the automated decision system changes.
section_path: Directive on Automated Decision-Making > Directive on Automated Decision-Making > Section 6.1 Algorithmic impact assessment
licence: Open Government Licence – Canada

text: Providing a meaningful explanation to clients of how and why the decision was made. For a decision that results in the denial of a benefit or service, a more detailed plain-language explanation is provided to the client, including the principal factors that led to the output and how that output was used by human officers. Explanations must also inform clients of relevant recourse options.
section_path: Directive on Automated Decision-Making > Directive on Automated Decision-Making > Section 6.2.3 Explanation
licence: Open Government Licence – Canada

text: Ensuring that the automated decision system allows for human involvement. At higher impact levels the final decision must be made by a human. Decisions cannot be made without having clearly defined human involvement during the decision-making process. Humans review the decisions or recommendations made by the system for accuracy and appropriateness and can intervene.
section_path: Directive on Automated Decision-Making > Directive on Automated Decision-Making > Section 6.3.13 Ensuring human involvement
licence: Open Government Licence – Canada

text: Consulting with the department's legal services from the concept stage of an automation project to ensure that the use of the automated decision system is compliant with applicable legal requirements.
section_path: Directive on Automated Decision-Making > Directive on Automated Decision-Making > Section 6.3.12 Legal services
licence: Open Government Licence – Canada

text: Informing clients of recourse options to challenge the administrative decision. Ensuring that recourse options are timely, effective, and easy to access.
section_path: Directive on Automated Decision-Making > Directive on Automated Decision-Making > Section 6.4 Recourse
licence: Open Government Licence – Canada

text: Excerpts from the GOV.UK Service Manual. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/service-standard and https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/helping-people-to-use-your-service/testing-for-accessibility Licence: Open Government Licence v3.0. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.
section_path: GOV.UK Service Standard > GOV.UK Service Standard
licence: Open Government Licence v3.0

text: Work towards creating a service that solves a whole problem for users, working with other teams and organisations where necessary. Design and develop your service around the needs of users, not around technologies or pre-selected solutions. This includes generative artificial intelligence and commercial off-the-shelf products. Users should not have to understand how government works in order to use public services.
section_path: GOV.UK Service Standard > GOV.UK Service Standard > Point 2 Solve a whole problem for users
licence: Open Government Licence v3.0

text: Provide a joined up experience across all channels. Test all the parts of the service that the user interacts with, online parts and offline parts like letters. A person who cannot finish in the automated channel still needs a consistent route through the staffed channel.
section_path: GOV.UK Service Standard > GOV.UK Service Standard > Point 3 Provide a joined up experience across all channels
licence: Open Government Licence v3.0

text: Build a service that is simple, intuitive and comprehensible. And test it with users to make sure it works for them. Make sure the service helps the user to do the thing they need to do as simply as possible, so that people succeed first time, with the minimum of help.
section_path: GOV.UK Service Standard > GOV.UK Service Standard > Point 4 Make the service simple to use
licence: Open Government Licence v3.0

text: Make sure the service works with the most common assistive technologies, screen readers or speech recognition software for example, and test the service with disabled users and with older users. Meet level AA of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines as a minimum. Think about accessibility from the start, including people who use a dialect or a language other than the one the model was tuned on.
section_path: GOV.UK Service Standard > GOV.UK Service Standard > Point 5 Make sure everyone can use the service
licence: Open Government Licence v3.0

text: Operate a reliable service. When the digital channel fails, users still need to complete the task. Reliability includes a staffed fallback and a published account of performance, not only an uptime figure for the model host.
section_path: GOV.UK Service Standard > GOV.UK Service Standard > Point 14 Operate a reliable service
licence: Open Government Licence v3.0

text: This briefing is an original summary. It is not the text of the Standard. The Standard is published by the UK government under the Open Government Licence v3.0. URL: https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard Licence of this briefing: CC0. The Standard itself is not copied here.
section_path: Briefing on the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard > Briefing on the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard
licence: CC0 briefing. The Standard is Open Government Licence v3.0 and is not copied in full.

text: The Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard asks public bodies to publish a record of an algorithmic tool that supports a decision. The record names the tool, the decision it supports, the data it uses, the points where a person reviews the output, and a contact for someone affected by the decision. Publishing the record does not itself authorise the decision.
section_path: Briefing on the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard > Briefing on the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard > What a record contains
licence: CC0 briefing. The Standard is Open Government Licence v3.0 and is not copied in full.

text: A transparency record is not a mandate. It does not grant a power to deny a benefit, and it does not replace an explanation to the person who was refused. It tells the public that the tool exists and how a human remains in the decision.
section_path: Briefing on the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard > Briefing on the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard > Limits of the record
licence: CC0 briefing. The Standard is Open Government Licence v3.0 and is not copied in full.

text: United States Office of Management and Budget memorandum M-24-10, Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence, 28 March 2024, is a public-domain federal work. URL: https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/M-24-10-Advancing-Governance-Innovation-and-Risk-Management-for-Agency-Use-of-Artificial-Intelligence.pdf This file is an original briefing of that memorandum, not a substitute for it. Licence of this briefing: CC0. The memorandum itself is in the public domain.
section_path: Briefing of OMB memorandum M-24-10 > Briefing of OMB memorandum M-24-10
licence: CC0 briefing. The memorandum is a US government work in the public domain.

text: M-24-10 distinguishes safety-impacting and rights-impacting uses of artificial intelligence. A system that helps decide a benefit, a right, or access to a public programme is rights-impacting. Minimum practices include an impact assessment before deployment, testing in the real operational context, and ongoing monitoring after the system is in use.
section_path: Briefing of OMB memorandum M-24-10 > Briefing of OMB memorandum M-24-10 > Rights-impacting uses
licence: CC0 briefing. The memorandum is a US government work in the public domain.

text: The memorandum expects a human fallback when the system fails or when a person asks for review of a rights-impacting decision. An outage of a vendor-hosted model does not suspend that duty. The agency still needs a way to continue the service and to report the incident. Data processed in a foreign vendor region remains subject to the agency's residency and privacy review.
section_path: Briefing of OMB memorandum M-24-10 > Briefing of OMB memorandum M-24-10 > Human fallback and incidents
licence: CC0 briefing. The memorandum is a US government work in the public domain.

text: Excerpt from NIST AI 100-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, January 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1 This is a United States government work in the public domain. The extract below is taken from section 5.4 and from the description of the Core. Line-break hyphenation in the source PDF has been rejoined.
section_path: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 > NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0
licence: Public domain (United States government work). Excerpt.

text: The AI RMF Core is composed of four functions: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE. GOVERN is a cross-cutting function. MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE can be applied in system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle. The functions organise risk management activities to govern, map, measure, and manage AI risks.
section_path: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 > NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 > Core functions
licence: Public domain (United States government work). Excerpt.

text: The MANAGE function entails allocating risk resources to mapped and measured risks on a regular basis and as defined by the GOVERN function. Risk treatment comprises plans to respond to, recover from, and communicate about incidents or events. After completing the MANAGE function, plans for prioritizing risk and regular monitoring and improvement will be in place. Framework users will have enhanced capacity to manage the risks of deployed AI systems. It is incumbent on Framework users to continue to apply the MANAGE function to deployed AI systems as methods, contexts, risks, and needs or expectations from relevant AI actors evolve over time.
section_path: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 > NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 > Section 5.4 Manage
licence: Public domain (United States government work). Excerpt.

text: MANAGE 4.3: Incidents and errors are communicated to relevant AI actors, including affected communities. Processes for tracking, responding to, and recovering from incidents and errors are followed and documented. Post-deployment monitoring includes appeal and override, decommissioning, incident response, recovery, and change management. Energy used by a standby region is part of the operational context of that recovery plan.
section_path: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 > NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 > Manage incidents and errors
licence: Public domain (United States government work). Excerpt.

text: NIST AI 600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, is a United States government publication in the public domain. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1 This file is an original briefing, not the full profile. Licence of this briefing: CC0.
section_path: Briefing of NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI profile > Briefing of NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI profile
licence: CC0 briefing. NIST AI 600-1 is a US government work in the public domain.

text: The Generative AI profile treats prompt injection as a risk to systems that read untrusted text. An untrusted message can carry an instruction that tries to override the system's task, for example by telling the system to disclose a record or to ignore its policy. A pre-processor screen should flag that pattern before the model acts on it. A canary string planted only in the untrusted message is a test that the instruction was not copied into an action.
section_path: Briefing of NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI profile > Briefing of NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI profile > Prompt injection
licence: CC0 briefing. NIST AI 600-1 is a US government work in the public domain.

text: The profile also treats confabulation, sometimes called hallucination, as a risk that a generative system will state a rule or a fee that no instrument contains. Content provenance and a human check are the controls the profile points to before such a statement is shown to the public.
section_path: Briefing of NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI profile > Briefing of NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI profile > Confabulation and provenance
licence: CC0 briefing. NIST AI 600-1 is a US government work in the public domain.

text: Short excerpts. Source: EUR-Lex, CELEX 32024R1689. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689 © European Union, 2024. Reuse is authorised provided the source is acknowledged. These are operative excerpts, not the full regulation.
section_path: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), excerpts > Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act
licence: © European Union, 2024. Reuse authorised with attribution (EUR-Lex).

text: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use. Human oversight shall aim to prevent or minimise the risks to health, safety or fundamental rights that may emerge when a high-risk AI system is used.
section_path: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), excerpts > Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act > Article 14 Human oversight
licence: © European Union, 2024. Reuse authorised with attribution (EUR-Lex).

text: Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect. Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake shall disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated.
section_path: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), excerpts > Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act > Article 50 Transparency
licence: © European Union, 2024. Reuse authorised with attribution (EUR-Lex).

text: Annex III lists high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2). Point 5 covers access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits. Point 5(a) covers AI systems intended to be used by public authorities or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, as well as to grant, reduce, revoke, or reclaim such benefits and services.
section_path: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), excerpts > Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act > Annex III point 5 Essential public services
licence: © European Union, 2024. Reuse authorised with attribution (EUR-Lex).

text: Short excerpts. Source: EUR-Lex, CELEX 32016R0679. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32016R0679 © European Union, 2016. Reuse is authorised provided the source is acknowledged.
section_path: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), excerpts > Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the General Data Protection Regulation
licence: © European Union, 2016. Reuse authorised with attribution (EUR-Lex).

text: Personal data shall be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject. Personal data shall be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes. Personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
section_path: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), excerpts > Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the General Data Protection Regulation > Article 5 Principles
licence: © European Union, 2016. Reuse authorised with attribution (EUR-Lex).

text: The data subject shall have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her. The data controller shall implement suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and freedoms and legitimate interests, at least the right to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller, to express his or her point of view and to contest the decision.
section_path: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), excerpts > Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the General Data Protection Regulation > Article 22 Automated individual decision-making
licence: © European Union, 2016. Reuse authorised with attribution (EUR-Lex).

text: In the case of a personal data breach, the controller shall without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority competent in accordance with Article 55, unless the personal data breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.
section_path: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), excerpts > Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the General Data Protection Regulation > Article 33 Notification of a breach
licence: © European Union, 2016. Reuse authorised with attribution (EUR-Lex).

text: When the personal data breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall communicate the personal data breach to the data subject without undue delay. The communication shall describe in clear and plain language the nature of the personal data breach and the measures taken or proposed to address it.
section_path: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), excerpts > Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the General Data Protection Regulation > Article 34 Communication to the data subject
licence: © European Union, 2016. Reuse authorised with attribution (EUR-Lex).

text: The Recommendation was adopted by UNESCO in 2021. URL: https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000381137 The official text is not reproduced. This briefing is original and is licensed CC0.
section_path: Briefing on the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence > Briefing on the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
licence: CC0 briefing. The UNESCO Recommendation text is not reproduced.

text: The UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI calls for inclusive access and non-discrimination in the design of public AI services. A public assistant that answers only in one standard language, or that cannot be used with a screen reader, fails that inclusion principle even when the underlying model is accurate for other users. Member states are encouraged to promote linguistic diversity and to assess impacts on persons with disabilities.
section_path: Briefing on the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence > Briefing on the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence > Inclusion and language
licence: CC0 briefing. The UNESCO Recommendation text is not reproduced.

text: The Recommendation ties AI in public services to proportionality, safety, and human oversight. An automated denial of a social benefit is the kind of decision the Recommendation expects a person to be able to understand and to challenge. The briefing does not restate country-specific obligations.
section_path: Briefing on the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence > Briefing on the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence > Proportionality and oversight
licence: CC0 briefing. The UNESCO Recommendation text is not reproduced.

text: The OECD AI Principles were adopted in 2019 and revised in 2024. URL: https://oecd.ai/en/ai-principles The official instrument is not reproduced. This briefing is original and is licensed CC0.
section_path: Briefing on the OECD AI Principles > Briefing on the OECD AI Principles
licence: CC0 briefing. The OECD instrument is not reproduced.

text: The OECD AI Principles ask that AI systems respect human rights and fairness, that they are transparent, and that they are robust, secure and safe. Accountability sits with the organisations that deploy them. A public-service assistant that invents a rule, or that reuses assistance logs for a new fraud purpose, is outside those principles until a person can explain the purpose and the safeguard.
section_path: Briefing on the OECD AI Principles > Briefing on the OECD AI Principles > Values and accountability
licence: CC0 briefing. The OECD instrument is not reproduced.

text: The principles treat international cooperation as a way to develop interoperable governance, not as a reason for one administration to copy another's institutional chart. Sandboxes and shared reporting of incidents are named as practical tools.
section_path: Briefing on the OECD AI Principles > Briefing on the OECD AI Principles > International cooperation
licence: CC0 briefing. The OECD instrument is not reproduced.

text: The Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme (Australia) reported in July 2023. Official report: https://robodebt.royalcommission.gov.au/ The report text is not reproduced. This briefing is original and is licensed CC0. It records publicly reported findings for use as a global example.
section_path: Briefing on the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme > Briefing on the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme
licence: CC0 briefing. The Royal Commission report is not reproduced.

text: Robodebt used automated income averaging to raise social-security debts. The Royal Commission found the scheme was unlawful. Debts were asserted against people without a sufficient legal basis and without a meaningful human check of the individual file before the debt was raised. The harm was not a rare model error. It was a system that treated an averaged figure as if it were proof.
section_path: Briefing on the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme > Briefing on the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme > Automated debts
licence: CC0 briefing. The Royal Commission report is not reproduced.

text: The global lesson is domain-level. An assistant that denies a benefit or asserts a debt needs a cited legal basis, an explanation a person can use, and a human review path that can stop the decision. Publishing a model card after the fact does not supply that path.
section_path: Briefing on the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme > Briefing on the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme > What later programmes should take from it
licence: CC0 briefing. The Royal Commission report is not reproduced.

text: The Hague District Court, 5 February 2020, ECLI:NL:RBDHA:2020:1878, stopped the Dutch SyRI legislation. Judgment: https://uitspraken.rechtspraak.nl/details?id=ECLI:NL:RBDHA:2020:1878 The judgment text is not reproduced. This briefing is original and is licensed CC0.
section_path: Briefing on the SyRI judgment > Briefing on the SyRI judgment
licence: CC0 briefing. The judgment text is not reproduced.

text: SyRI was a system for linking public-service data and scoring neighbourhoods and people for a risk of social-security fraud. The court held that the legislation did not meet Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The interference with private life was not proportionate, and the system was not transparent enough for a person to understand or to challenge how a risk score was produced.
section_path: Briefing on the SyRI judgment > Briefing on the SyRI judgment > Risk scores for social-security fraud
licence: CC0 briefing. The judgment text is not reproduced.

text: Data collected to administer a benefit were drawn into a fraud score. That change of purpose, hidden inside a cross-domain collector, is the part of the case later programmes still trip over. A new score needs its own legal basis. An instruction to reuse the logs does not create one.
section_path: Briefing on the SyRI judgment > Briefing on the SyRI judgment > Purpose and the source of the data
licence: CC0 briefing. The judgment text is not reproduced.

text: The Dutch parliamentary inquiry into childcare benefits reported in 2020 under the title Ongekend onrecht. Inquiry: https://www.tweedekamer.nl/kamerstukken/detail?id=2020Z25785 The report text is not reproduced. This briefing is original and is licensed CC0.
section_path: Briefing on the Dutch childcare-benefits inquiry > Briefing on the Dutch childcare-benefits inquiry
licence: CC0 briefing. The inquiry report is not reproduced.

text: The tax authority used risk models in the childcare-benefits system and wrongly treated thousands of families as fraudulent. Dual nationality was used as a risk signal. Families were ordered to repay benefits. The inquiry documented the harm of a model that combined an assistance file with a fraud objective and then left people without a usable explanation.
section_path: Briefing on the Dutch childcare-benefits inquiry > Briefing on the Dutch childcare-benefits inquiry > Risk models and wrongful recovery
licence: CC0 briefing. The inquiry report is not reproduced.

text: The same administration was trying to pay a benefit and to detect fraud. Those objectives conflicted, and the conflict was resolved by the model rather than by a published rule. A later assistant that is told to ship a fraud score on top of an assistance log repeats that pattern unless the conflict is documented and the new purpose is refused until it has a legal basis.
section_path: Briefing on the Dutch childcare-benefits inquiry > Briefing on the Dutch childcare-benefits inquiry > Conflicting objectives
licence: CC0 briefing. The inquiry report is not reproduced.

text: The Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI was published in 2024 by the AI Verify Foundation and the Infocomm Media Development Authority. URL: https://aiverifyfoundation.sg/resources/model-ai-governance-framework-for-generative-ai/ The framework text is not reproduced. This briefing is original and is licensed CC0.
section_path: Briefing on the Singapore Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI > Briefing on the Singapore Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI
licence: CC0 briefing. The framework text is not reproduced.

text: The framework treats content provenance as a control for synthetic impersonation. A public body that publishes generative replies should be able to show that an official answer came from the official system, and a fake ministry chatbot collecting identity numbers should be distinguishable from that channel. Provenance is a distribution problem as well as a model problem: the mark has to travel with the message.
section_path: Briefing on the Singapore Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI > Briefing on the Singapore Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI > Content provenance
licence: CC0 briefing. The framework text is not reproduced.

text: The framework also expects testing against abusive prompts and a way to report incidents when a generative system states a fact or a rule it should not state. Those controls sit beside accountability: the organisation that deploys the system remains responsible for the reply.
section_path: Briefing on the Singapore Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI > Briefing on the Singapore Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI > Testing and incidents
licence: CC0 briefing. The framework text is not reproduced.

text: The Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS No. 225) was opened for signature in 2024. URL: https://www.coe.int/en/web/artificial-intelligence/the-framework-convention-on-artificial-intelligence The treaty text is not reproduced. This briefing is original and is licensed CC0.
section_path: Briefing on the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence > Briefing on the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence
licence: CC0 briefing. The treaty text is not reproduced.

text: The Framework Convention requires parties to address risks to human rights, democracy and the rule of law across the lifecycle of an AI system. For a public-service assistant that denies a benefit, that means a remedy a person can actually use, not only an internal log. Transparency and accountability are duties of the deployer, including when a vendor hosts the model.
section_path: Briefing on the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence > Briefing on the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence > Human dignity and remedies
licence: CC0 briefing. The treaty text is not reproduced.

text: The Convention leaves room for sandboxes so that public bodies can test a system before it touches a live decision. A sandbox is not a substitute for a mandate. It is where a refusal, a breach notification, and a human-review path can be exercised without spending public money on a live mistake.
section_path: Briefing on the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence > Briefing on the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence > Safe innovation
licence: CC0 briefing. The treaty text is not reproduced.

text: ITU-T Y.3172: Architectural Framework for Machine Learning in Future Networks Including IMT-2020 Summary of Key Content (referenced in the AI Readiness Framework): 1. SCOPE ITU-T Y.3172 specifies an architectural framework for machine learning (ML) in future networks including IMT-2020. It defines the ML pipeline architecture with nodes and interfaces for integrating ML into network operations. 2. ML PIPELINE NODES (from Figure 3, Section 8.1) The standard defines 7 nodes in the ML pipeline plus 2 supporting components: Pipeline Nodes (in order): - SRC (Source): The source of data that can be used as input to the ML pipeline. Potential SRC nodes include user equipment (UE), session management function (SMF), and application function (AF). - C (Collector): Responsible for collecting data from one or more SRC nodes. A collector node may have the capability to configure SRC nodes (e.g., control the nature of data, its granularity and periodicity). - PP (Pre-processor): Responsible for data cleaning, transformation, normalisation, and feature engineering. Prepares raw data for ML consumption. May also perform data format conversion. - M (Model): Where ML models are trained, validated, and execute inference. Includes model selection, training, evaluation, and serving. Supports supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning. - P (Policy): Enforces policies on ML output before distribution. Ensures ML decisions comply with network operator policies, safety constraints, and regulatory requirements. - D (Distributor): Distributes the output of the ML model to one or more SINK nodes. Handles routing of ML results to appropriate targets. - SINK (Target of ML output): Where inference results are applied — actuators, control plane, decision systems, dashboards, or feedback loops. ML output may be policies or configurations applied to the network. Supporting Components: - MLFO (ML Function Orchestrator): A logical node that manages and orchestrates all nodes in the ML pipeline. Receives ML intent as input and coordinates the pipeline execution. - ML Sandbox: A validation environment where ML models can be trained, tested, and their effects on the network evaluated. Uses simulated ML underlay networks. Designed to prevent ML applications from affecting the live network. 3. ML PIPELINE FLOW Pipeline: SRC → C → PP → M → P → D → SINK With ML Sandbox running in parallel using simulated underlay networks. MLFO orchestrates the entire pipeline based on ML intent. 4. DATA HANDLING REFERENCE POINTS The architecture defines 4 data handling reference points: - Reference Point 1: Between SINK and ML underlay networks
section_path: Summary of ITU-T Y.3172
licence: MIT, as part of ITUAIReadiness. This is a summary, not the ITU-T Recommendation.

text: → M → P → D → SINK With ML Sandbox running in parallel using simulated underlay networks. MLFO orchestrates the entire pipeline based on ML intent. 4. DATA HANDLING REFERENCE POINTS The architecture defines 4 data handling reference points: - Reference Point 1: Between SINK and ML underlay networks (data output) - Reference Point 2: Between ML Sandbox and simulated ML underlay networks - Reference Point 3: Between SRC and ML underlay networks (data input) - Reference Point 4: Between SINK and ML underlay networks 5. HIGH-LEVEL ARCHITECTURAL REQUIREMENTS (Section 7) Five categories of requirements: - REQ-ML-COR: Enablers for correlation — support correlation of data from multiple sources, multiple technologies, distributed instantiation - REQ-ML-DEP: Enablers for deployment — define interaction points, support split/combined deployments, flexible placement, plug-and-play data sources - REQ-ML-INT: Interface-related — support model transfer, data transfer for training, standard APIs, data sharing mechanisms - REQ-ML-SPEC: Declarative specifications — standard ML application representation, specification of data sources/model repos/targets/constraints, flexible split, third-party specifications - REQ-ML-MNG: Management of ML functionalities — model selection, training/updates, monitoring, orchestration, flexible chaining 6. RELEVANCE TO AI READINESS FRAMEWORK - Dimension 1 (Data/Model Marketplace): SRC and C nodes relate to data collection and marketplace infrastructure - Dimension 3 (Cross-Domain Correlation): REQ-ML-COR requirements directly map to cross-domain data correlation - Dimension 5 (AI Integration in Workflows): The full pipeline (SRC→C→PP→M→P→D→SINK) provides the standard for AI integration - Dimension 7 (Strategy Alignment): MLFO and ML intent map to strategic coordination and intent-based management - Dimension 10 (AI & Policies): P (Policy) node and ML Sandbox map to policy evaluation and sandboxing in AI lifecycle - Dimension 13 (Digital Infrastructure): Y.3172 nodes map to physical infrastructure requirements (compute, networking, edge) Node-to-Factor Mapping: - Data factor → SRC, C, PP (data collection, aggregation, preparation) - Research factor → M (model training, validation, evaluation) - Standards factor → P, MLFO (policy enforcement, orchestration standards) - Deployment factor → D, SINK (distribution, deployment of ML output) - Sandbox factor → ML Sandbox (testing in simulated environments) - OpenSource factor → M (open-source model availability, model marketplace) 7. ENERGY CONSIDERATIONS The standard also addresses energy characteristics of pipeline nodes, relevant to Energy AI Readiness metrics under Dimension 13.

text: EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) - Summary 1. OVERVIEW The EU AI Act is the first comprehensive legal framework on AI worldwide. It entered into force on 1 August 2024 and will be fully applicable by 2 August 2026, with phased implementation. 2. RISK-BASED CLASSIFICATION The Act classifies AI systems into four risk tiers: a) Unacceptable Risk (Prohibited): Social scoring by governments, real-time biometric identification in public spaces (with exceptions), manipulation techniques, exploitation of vulnerabilities. Effective from Feb 2025. b) High Risk: AI in critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, justice. Requires conformity assessments, risk management, data governance, transparency, human oversight. c) Limited Risk: Chatbots, deepfakes, emotion recognition. Must meet transparency obligations (users must know they interact with AI). d) Minimal Risk: Spam filters, AI in video games. No specific obligations. 3. GENERAL PURPOSE AI (GPAI) MODELS - All GPAI providers must provide technical documentation, comply with copyright law, publish training data summaries - Systemic risk GPAI (>10^25 FLOPs training compute): additional obligations including model evaluations, adversarial testing, incident reporting, cybersecurity measures 4. IMPLEMENTATION TIMELINE - Feb 2025: Prohibited practices and AI literacy in force - Aug 2025: GPAI model obligations in force - Aug 2026: Full application (high-risk AI in regulated products) - Aug 2027: Extended transition for some high-risk systems 5. GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE - European AI Office (within European Commission) - National competent authorities in each EU member state - AI Board (representatives from member states) - Advisory forum and scientific panel 6. PENALTIES - Up to 35M EUR or 7% of global turnover for prohibited AI practices - Up to 15M EUR or 3% for high-risk non-compliance - Up to 7.5M EUR or 1.5% for incorrect information 7. RELEVANCE TO ITU AI READINESS FRAMEWORK - Dimension 10 (AI & Policies): The most comprehensive regulatory framework globally; benchmark for policy evaluation - Dimension 7 (Strategy Alignment): EU-wide coordination mechanism - Dimension 5 (AI Integration): Compliance requirements affect how AI is integrated in workflows - Dimension 1 (Data Marketplace): Data governance requirements for high-risk AI - Dimension 6 (Human Interface): Transparency requirements for AI-human interaction - Provides a model for developing countries designing AI governance frameworks

text: ITU AI for Good Sandbox Network - Summary 1. OVERVIEW The ITU AI for Good Sandbox is a distributed, standards-based platform that lowers barriers to AI research, experimentation, and innovation. It provides cloud computing resources, datasets, and tools for AI experimentation aligned with ITU-T standards. 2. KEY CAPABILITIES - Cloud credit support for AI experimentation projects - Access to computing resources (GPU/CPU) for model training - Hosting environment for AI models and datasets - Sandbox environments for testing AI solutions in controlled settings - Integration with ITU-T standards for interoperability 3. SANDBOX NETWORK VISION - Distributed network of sandboxes across regions and countries - Standards-based (ITU-T Y.3172) pipeline architecture - Enables collaboration across countries and domains - Bridges gap between open science, research, and standardization - Local deployment capability for data sovereignty 4. USE CASES SUPPORTED - AI model training and validation - Policy impact simulation and extrapolation - Domain-specific AI testing (healthcare, agriculture, disaster management) - Cross-domain correlation analysis - GenAI content generation and evaluation 5. RELEVANCE TO ITU AI READINESS FRAMEWORK - The Sandbox is the primary hosting environment for the AI-RE Toolkit - Dimension 10 (AI & Policies): Sandbox provides simulated timelines for policy what-if analysis - Dimension 11 (AI for Inclusion): Sandbox hosts digital twins and simulation environments - Factor 6 (Sandbox): Directly maps to the sandbox environments factor - Knowledge Base is hosted within the Sandbox infrastructure - Multiple toolkit instances can run in parallel, connected to the Sandbox for KB record transfer 6. PLUGFEST INTEGRATION - Cloud credits provided to selected Plugfest projects - Projects validated in sandbox environments - Results feed back into the AI Readiness Framework dimensions and metrics
